Some FHIR for Research workshops provide interactive Jupyter notebooks in addition to their rendered web pages. Choose an option based on whether you want to read the material or execute and modify its code.

## Recommended options

| Goal | Recommended option | Account required? | Notes |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Read the workshop | Rendered workshop page | No | Best for reading instructions and reviewing code without running it. |
| Run the workshop locally | Download the notebook and open it in JupyterLab Desktop | No | Recommended interactive option. Both Data Analysis/CDS notebooks have been verified to open successfully. |
| Use an existing Python setup | Local Jupyter or Visual Studio Code | No | Appropriate for users who already manage Python environments. |
| Run in a hosted environment | Google Colab | Google account | The corrected one-click link reaches the generated notebook. Follow organizational policy before using a personal or cloud account. |
| View a generated notebook | NBViewer | No | View only. The corrected link has been verified with a generated notebook. |
| Run in a temporary hosted environment | Binder | No | Not currently supported; the notebook deployment branch does not contain a Binder environment specification. |

## How the notebooks are published

The editable workshop sources are Quarto `.qmd` files. During deployment, Quarto generates `.ipynb` files and publishes them to the [`mitre/fhir-for-research`](https://github.com/mitre/fhir-for-research) mirror on its `gh-pages` branch.

Colab, NBViewer, and Binder must therefore use the generated notebook path on `gh-pages`, such as `workshops/data-analysis-cds/01-fhir-analysis.ipynb`. They should not use the source branch or add a `data/` directory to that path.

## JupyterLab Desktop (recommended)

[JupyterLab Desktop](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab-desktop) provides a local notebook environment without requiring a separately managed Jupyter server.

1. Install the appropriate [JupyterLab Desktop release](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab-desktop#installation) for your operating system.
2. On the workshop page, select **Download Notebook**.
3. Open the downloaded `.ipynb` file in JupyterLab Desktop.
4. Confirm that the notebook uses a Python 3 kernel.
5. Follow the notebook's dependency instructions before running the remaining cells.
6. Configure the required FHIR server URL when prompted by the notebook.

The Data Analysis and Genomics CDS notebooks have been verified to download and open in JupyterLab Desktop. Their complete cell execution still depends on access to a compatible FHIR server containing the workshop data.

## Local Jupyter

Use this option if Jupyter is already installed in a local Python environment.

1. Download the `.ipynb` file from the workshop page.
2. Activate the Python environment you want to use.
3. Start JupyterLab or Jupyter Notebook.
4. Open the downloaded notebook and select the matching Python kernel.
5. Follow the dependency and FHIR server instructions in the notebook.

See the [Project Jupyter installation guide](https://jupyter.org/install) for installation options.

## Visual Studio Code

[Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) can open and run `.ipynb` files with the [Jupyter extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-toolsai.jupyter).

1. Install Visual Studio Code, the Python extension, and the Jupyter extension.
2. Download the workshop notebook.
3. Open the `.ipynb` file in Visual Studio Code.
4. Select a Python environment with the required packages, or run the notebook's dependency cell.

This option has the same local dependency and FHIR server requirements as JupyterLab Desktop.

## Google Colab

[Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/) can open a generated notebook from the public GitHub mirror. A Google account is required to use a hosted runtime and save work.

Use the **Open in Colab** button on the notebook page. The corrected link for the FHIR Data Analysis notebook was verified to resolve successfully. If the button is unavailable, download the `.ipynb` file from the workshop page and import it with **File → Upload notebook**.

Opening the notebook does not guarantee that every cell will run. Complete execution still requires access to a compatible FHIR server containing the workshop data.

::: callout-warning
## Sensitive data and cloud services

Do not use Colab or another cloud notebook service with protected health information (PHI), personally identifiable information (PII), credentials, or a sensitive FHIR endpoint unless that service and account have been approved by your organization. Use a local environment when handling sensitive data.
:::

## Viewing without execution

Use the rendered workshop page when you only need to read the material. NBViewer is another view-only option and now targets the generated notebook in the public mirror. The corrected NBViewer link was verified successfully with the FHIR Data Analysis notebook.

## Binder status

Binder can find and clone the generated notebook on the public mirror's `gh-pages` branch, but that branch contains only the published website and generated files. Binder stops with `No environment specification found` because the branch does not include the repository's dependency configuration.

Binder is therefore not a supported option for these notebooks. Supporting it would require publishing a compatible Binder environment specification alongside the generated notebooks or maintaining a separate Binder-ready branch.

## FHIR server and workshop data

Opening a notebook does not provide its FHIR data automatically. Complete execution requires a compatible FHIR server containing the data expected by that workshop.

The public HAPI FHIR server can be useful for basic connectivity tests, but it does not contain the workshop's expected dataset. For the repository's local test environment, see [Standing Up a FHIR Testing Server](../modules/synthea-test-server.qmd). That setup requires Docker.

## Other approaches evaluated

- **GitHub Codespaces** could provide a reproducible hosted development environment, but it would require a maintained development-container configuration and may introduce account, startup-time, and usage-limit considerations.
- **JupyterLite** runs notebooks entirely in a browser, but package compatibility and browser restrictions on remote FHIR requests need a proof of concept before it can be recommended.

These options are not currently supported workshop workflows.
